title: A Required Payment, Not a Gift
definition: A payment demanded under colonial authority.
content:
Tribute was a required payment under Spanish colonial authority. It was not simply a freely chosen present. Collecting it brought resources into the colonial system. To understand a demand, ask who required payment, who was expected to pay, and what rule applied in that place and period. A label such as tax does not tell us whether a collection was fair.

Imagine two fictional cards. One describes a family choosing a gift; the other records a payment demanded by an authority. The second describes an obligation: something people were required to do. Do not call it voluntary just because a record says it was paid. A payment record also does not show that every resident agreed with the demand. We study this system to understand people and power, not to reward collecting from classmates.

Open the three clues. Then choose the explanation they support. Use Explain if you want help, and return to the lesson before practice when a topic needs review.
clues: Tribute was demanded under colonial authority, rather than simply offered as a gift.
Collections supplied resources to the colonial system.
Recorded payment does not prove that a person approved of the demand.
task: A record says a required payment was collected. Which description fits?
A colonial obligation was recorded, not necessarily a voluntary gift
Every payer freely chose a gift
Every family agreed with the demand
The record proves every collection was fair
reason: A colonial obligation was recorded, not necessarily a voluntary gift. Recorded payment does not prove that a person approved of the demand.

title: Payments Could Involve Goods
definition: Giving products instead of coins to meet a payment demand.
content:
Payments did not always consist only of coins. Early colonial accounts describe goods such as rice, cotton, cloth and wax being collected as tribute in particular places. The kind of payment depended on the rule and setting. An example of cloth tribute does not mean that every household everywhere paid the same cloth or amount.

A study in The Philippine Review of Economics discusses woven goods in early tribute and trade. This helps keep the work of makers visible: cloth had to be produced before it could be collected. Our pictured bundle is a modern teaching symbol, not an original tribute item or a measurement guide. When you read a record, look for its place, date, item and unit. Do not change an example into a universal payment schedule.

Open the three clues. Then choose the explanation they support. Use Explain if you want help, and return to the lesson before practice when a topic needs review.
clues: Early accounts describe goods, including cloth and rice, in some tribute collections.
Products represent work and materials, not objects that appeared without effort.
A named item does not establish one amount or form for every community.
task: A source lists cloth in one early tribute collection. What can you conclude?
Goods could be involved in that setting; other collections need their own evidence
Every household paid identical cloth
Coins were never used anywhere
The illustration is an original tribute object
reason: Goods could be involved in that setting; other collections need their own evidence. A named item does not establish one amount or form for every community.

title: What Did a Payment Mean for a Household?
definition: A demand that takes resources or effort to meet.
content:
A required payment could affect what a household had available for its other needs. Goods required materials and work. Money required access to money. To explain the burden, we need more than the size of a demand: we also need to know what resources people had and what conditions they faced. This mission does not assign one experience to every family.

Try a fictional comparison, not a historical tax rate. Household A has ten supply tokens and Household B has five. Both must give two. A has eight left and B has three. The same number taken leaves different amounts available. The tokens stand for resources only; they are not pesos, real tribute rates or points earned for taking goods. To explain an actual case, find evidence about the demand and the household circumstances.

Open the three clues. Then choose the explanation they support. Use Explain if you want help, and return to the lesson before practice when a topic needs review.
clues: Ask what the household could draw on.
Equal amounts demanded do not automatically mean equal burdens.
task: In the token model, both households give two but start with different supplies. What does it illustrate?
The same demand can leave different resources available
Both households must face identical burdens
Two tokens was the historical tribute everywhere
Taking supplies earns more learning points
reason: The same demand can leave different resources available. Equal amounts demanded do not automatically mean equal burdens.

title: Read the Rule and the Collection Separately
definition: A record describing payments received or collected.
content:
A rule can describe what an authority demanded. A collection record can describe what was received. These are related questions, but they are not the same. A rule alone does not prove that every demanded payment was collected. A recorded collection alone does not settle whether it followed the rule or how it affected the people who paid.

Our fictional source desk has three cards: a payment instruction, a collection entry, and a complaint about an extra demand. The instruction helps identify the rule. The entry helps identify a recorded action. The complaint helps identify a reported problem; it does not by itself show how the problem was finally resolved. Compare the cards rather than treating any one as a complete account. Colonial writers had their own purposes, and their records may leave local voices out.

Open the three clues. Then choose the explanation they support. Use Explain if you want help, and return to the lesson before practice when a topic needs review.
clues: An instruction describes a demand, not proof that it was fully carried out.
A collection entry describes a recorded payment.
A complaint needs follow-up evidence to establish its outcome.
task: An instruction and a collection entry differ. What is the best next step?
Compare their dates, coverage and recorded actions before explaining the difference
Assume the instruction proves every collection
Treat a complaint as proof of its final outcome
Invent the missing payments
reason: Compare their dates, coverage and recorded actions before explaining the difference. A complaint needs follow-up evidence to establish its outcome.

title: Tax Rules Changed Over Time
definition: A change in the rules or system of taxation.
content:
Spanish colonial rule lasted for a long period, and taxation did not stay unchanged throughout it. Historian Filomeno Aguilars study identifies the ending of tribute in 1884 and the introduction of cedulas personales in 1885. A cedula personal was connected with a later personal-tax system. Keep these two stages distinct instead of treating every colonial payment as the same rule.

The study explains that the later system used rates connected with economic capacity. That does not mean taxation ended, that every person paid the same amount, or that everyone welcomed the change. Our timeline marks the transition described in this study; it is not a complete chart of every tax. A real payment record still needs its own date, category and setting. We are comparing historical systems, not giving instructions about modern taxes.

Open the three clues. Then choose the explanation they support. Use Explain if you want help, and return to the lesson before practice when a topic needs review.
clues: The study distinguishes the end of tribute in 1884 from the later cedula system in 1885.
Ending one form of taxation did not mean that all taxes ended.
A dated payment needs the rule that applied in its own setting.
task: A caption says ending tribute meant all colonial taxes disappeared. Which correction fits?
One system ended while a later personal-tax system followed
All taxes ended forever
Every earlier and later rate was identical
The dates prove universal approval
reason: One system ended while a later personal-tax system followed. A dated payment needs the rule that applied in its own setting.

title: Prepare Your Tribute Investigation Report
definition: A record describing payments received or collected.
content: Review five ideas from this mission. Tribute was a required colonial payment rather than simply a gift. Payments could include goods in particular settings. The burden depended on available resources as well as the demand. Rules and recorded collections answer different questions. Tax systems also changed over time. Prepare a fictional museum report for another Grade 5 learner. State what was demanded, identify the supporting source and explain what you cannot yet know. If you use the two-token household model, label it as a model. It is not a historical tribute rate. Do not assume all households had the same experience or that payment proves agreement. Your main quiz has five questions. Three correct passes this mission. If you need help, the review path leads back to learning content before targeted practice and a retry. Complete all missions, then pass the chapter challenge to earn the chapter badge.
clues: An instruction describes a demand, not proof that it was fully carried out.
A collection entry describes a recorded payment.
A complaint needs follow-up evidence to establish its outcome.
task: Which report best explains a tribute record?
Name the demand, use dated evidence and explain its limits
Treat one rate as universal for all centuries
Call every payment a freely chosen gift
Use model tokens as exact historical pesos
reason: Explain the demand with dated evidence and identify what the source does not establish.
